claims.text: The starting material is a homogeneous solution of noble-metal precursors in equimolar ratios.
Low-temperature solution-based techniques can synthesize HEA nanoparticles.
A chemically controlled solution environment permits precise adjustment of precursor reduction kinetics.
Differences in the reduction potentials and rates of metal precursors can lead to phase separation in HEA nanoparticles.
Synchronizing the reduction rates of multiple noble-metal precursors causes concurrent nucleation.
Concurrent nucleation rapidly produces uniformly mixed nascent alloy clusters.
Aligning the reduction onset of all precursors minimizes sequential reduction and elemental segregation.
Synchronized reduction produces a single homogeneous nucleation event.
A single homogeneous nucleation event freezes the multimetal mixture into a uniform high-entropy state at low temperature.
Synchronized low-temperature reduction will produce HEA nanoparticles having a homogeneous solid-solution phase with minimal phase separation.
High-temperature shock synthesis commonly produces phase segregation because precursor reduction rates differ.
Conventional high-temperature methods often yield nonuniform elemental distributions and phase separation.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to noble metal-based HEA nanoparticles made under controlled chemical-reduction conditions.
The mechanism may fail when constituent metals have extremely disparate reduction potentials.
The mechanism may fail when support-surface interactions dominate nucleation and growth.
High-temperature shock approaches face scale-up limitations because of instrument and support-stability requirements.
Whether synchronized reduction controls homogeneity across different noble-metal combinations remains uncertain.
Failure of the low-temperature samples to improve elemental homogeneity and phase uniformity relative to the high-temperature control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The experiment says reduction kinetics are the only variable and that all other parameters are identical, but it compares a low-temperature solution process with a conventional high-temperature method. Temperature and potentially the synthesis method therefore change along with reduction kinetics.
